seen.cipher: The six lines are Chinook Jargon written in ordinary script, with English words mixed in: 'Wake siyah cultus mitlite nesika conoway ... tum-tum ... rebels puck puck nesika tomolloh ... devils. Klosh nanitch conoway sun tomolloh. Klahawyum mika?' The hand is large and every word is legible at this size; no letter or number substitution is used.

2050.closed: Not a cipher. Ingalls wrote to Senator Nesmith of Oregon in Chinook Jargon, the Pacific Northwest trade language (that both men knew it from Oregon service is our background knowledge, not checked here): 'nesika' we, 'conoway' all, 'tum-tum' heart, 'tomolloh' tomorrow, 'kloshe nanitch' look out, 'klahowya mika' how are you. The catalogue's 'Union cipher letter' is a cataloguer's word for an unfamiliar language. Read on the 400 px public preview; the hand is large enough for every word, but a subscriber view of the full scan would confirm it.

seen.extent: Four U.S. Military Telegraph forms of 1-3 July 1863, each 10 to 18 lines of words: .339 (Camp Piatt, 1 July, to 'Operator'), .229 and .341 (Fayette, 2 July, to 'Thomas', signed 'Graham') and .344 (Fayette, 3 July, 9.35 pm, to 'Thomas', signed 'Graham', '55' words).
seen.cipher: Union route cipher of the Stager type: English plain words in transposed order mixed with code words and nulls ('Florida ... says ... point Rye sycamore reported miller there fifth ... amazon July ... wife and Lewisburg ... soldier had twenty yesterday', .341). The docket of .341 reads 'Col. C.B. White / Statement of Mrs. Miller / about 22nd & 45th Va', so 'Graham' is Colonel Carr B. White, 12th Ohio. GLC02414.114 is the same message written out word by word in the route grid ('Fayette July second Scammon Charleston ... Lewisburg yesterday ... White'), the period decipherment of .341. For .229, .339 and .344 no decoded copy was found among the siblings listed.

1301.unvetted: Narváez's 'Dos criptosistemas empleados por el coronel José A. Torrens en Colombia (1825-1826)', Memorias de la Academia Mexicana de la Historia 49 (2007-08) 7-43, is not online, and the notes are in the SRE archive. What is now known: notes 2 (23 Jan) and 3 (9 Apr 1826) are wholly in Torrens's 10 x 7 matrix cipher, whose key sheet survives (AHDSREM exp. 5-16-8615 ff. 27-29) and is printed in EHMCM 38 (2009) p. 142; Narváez says several messages Torrens enciphered this way are already printed in books. So the cipher part is almost certainly read; the code part is unknown.
